seo.title: Karmic tail 21 22 19 compatibility: The World, The Fool, The Sun
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 22 19 compatibility: a whole shared world at the entry, the Fool's play in the middle and a main task of stepping into direct light.

title: Karmic tail 21-22-19 in compatibility: a couple who must step into the light
short: The couple's karmic tail 21-22-19 holds the last three cards of the deck, The World, The Fool and The Sun, in an odd order: the couple starts where the deck ends, steps over its edge and comes back to The Sun. The answer lies in the roles of the points. At the entry the two want a whole shared world; they live the middle like The Fool, lightly, in play, without naming what they are to each other; and the main task is The Sun: to step into direct light and say aloud what has long been plain to see.

sections.h2: Three cards in one line from the fool
paragraphs: The plot fits into a few lines. A ship is wrecked off the coast of Illyria. A girl who survives, Viola, dresses as a young man, takes the name Cesario and enters the service of Duke Orsino as his page. The Duke is hopelessly in love with the Countess Olivia and sends the new page to her with his declarations. Olivia falls in love with the page. The page is in love with the Duke and says nothing. The knot is untied by Viola's twin brother Sebastian, whom she believed drowned.

Halfway through the play Viola meets the fool, Feste. He serves Olivia but moves freely between the two houses, and Viola remarks that she saw him at the Duke's. The fool answers: "Foolery, sir, does walk about the orb like the sun; it shines everywhere." The orb is the globe, the world itself. The World, The Fool and The Sun in one sentence, in the same order as in the tail 21-22-19. And it is said to someone who walks her whole road in a mask.

The title is a clue too. Twelfth Night is the last night of the Christmas season, the eve of Epiphany. The Royal Shakespeare Company describes it as a time of revelry in which the norms of society were inverted. The next morning came the feast of appearing: the Greek epiphaneia means "appearance". The play is named after the night before the light. And its second title, What You Will, simply means "whatever you wish": the very thing a couple brings to the entry of its task.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 21 — The World: a love "more noble than the world"
paragraphs: The play opens in the voice of The World. "If music be the food of love, play on, / Give me excess of it," the Duke demands. His own love, he says, is "more noble than the world" and "all as hungry as the sea". This is a wish not for a part but for the whole. In Yuliana Lisovskaya's reading, the entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language.

Viola and the Duke find their common language at once. "He hath known you but three days, and already you are no stranger," a courtier marvels. The Duke tells his page: "Thou know'st no less but all; I have unclasp'd / To thee the book even of my secret soul," and promises: "thou shalt live as freely as thy lord, / To call his fortunes thine." A whole world for two in three days.

It is easy to recognise the start of a 21-22-19 couple here. In the first weeks comes the feeling of having known each other all their lives. Talk until dawn, one way of seeing things, plans "not like everyone else's": move to the sea, travel half the world, live by their own rules. In the compatibility reading the same point also appears in the sphere "Relationship and common language", and there The World is the couple's common language.

But the entry point lies on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. The play holds two closed worlds. The Duke admits, "I myself am best / When least in company," sends messengers to the woman he loves and stays among his music: "Love-thoughts lie rich when canopied with bowers." Olivia has vowed that "The element itself, till seven years' heat, / Shall not behold her face at ample view." And in the very first scene the Duke tells the spirit of love that its capacity "Receiveth as the sea", yet whatever enters "falls into abatement and low price / Even in a minute!" A whole world that no outsider enters, where nothing keeps its worth for more than a minute, is no longer open space but a fence.

In a couple this looks ordinary. Friends drift away; relatives see the two only on holidays. The shared plans are so big that they are frightening to start: the couple discusses a trip round the world, not next Tuesday. Each is sure the other already understands, so nothing has been agreed out loud. Understanding is mistaken for an agreement.

Feste sums this point up in a single line. Men like the Duke, he advises, should be put to sea, "that their business might be everything, and their intent everywhere, for that's it that always makes a good voyage of nothing." Everything, everywhere, nothing. This is the passage from The World to The Fool, from the card of fullness to the card Waite marks with a zero.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 22 — The Fool: friendship under a false name
paragraphs: Viola lives through the middle of the play as The Fool, and calls herself one. When Olivia hints that the page is not what he seems, Viola answers: "Then think you right; I am not what I am." A moment later: "now I am your fool." Page and master become best friends: the Duke trusts the page with everything, they listen to the fool's songs together and argue about love. The difference in rank does not get in their way, but it gives their closeness no name. Who they are to each other nobody knows, themselves included.

This is what The Fool looks like in the middle of a couple's tail. The lightness here is not stupidity but skill. "This fellow is wise enough to play the fool," Viola says of Feste, and then: "For folly, that he wisely shows, is fit." Waite describes his Fool the same way: "His countenance is full of intelligence and expectant dream." A couple with this middle has trust, freedom, humour, the ability to start from zero and not to cling to status. Two people like best friends who find each other interesting.

The minus is the same lightness. Years together, and still "we just live together". A serious talk turns into a joke; a conflict is solved by a move, a new project, a new trip. Everything begins easily, and at the first step that requires naming the relationship in front of witnesses, the two step back. From outside they could pass for neighbours who get on well.

Feste jokes about it outright: "fools are as like husbands as pilchards are to herrings, the husband's the bigger." The middle of this tail stands exactly between play and marriage, and a couple can go a long time without noticing which side it is on.

The numbers say the same about the middle. By the arithmetic of the edges another arcanum would stand there: 21 + 19 = 40, 4 + 0 = 4 — The Emperor: order, clear roles, status. But the couple's middle is built not from the edges but from the middles of the two personal tails, and it comes out as The Fool. The form that could have been calculated never appears in this tail.

In 92% of such couples The Fool in the middle is made of 5 and 17: one partner's Hierophant and the other's Star. In Waite's divinatory list The Hierophant opens with "Marriage, alliance", and The Star has "hope and bright prospects". Our reading: in the middle a habit of form meets hope, and together they make not a form but a road. The play acts this sum out literally: Feste puts on a gown and a beard to play Sir Topas the curate. The Fool in The Hierophant's clothes.

sections.h2: Main task, 19 — The Sun: "A blank, my lord"
paragraphs: The quietest scene in the play is the most exact one for the main task. The Duke and his page are alone. Orsino insists that no woman could love as he does. Viola objects and tells a story: "My father had a daughter loved a man, / As it might be perhaps, were I a woman, / I should your lordship." — "And what's her history?" — "A blank, my lord. She never told her love, / But let concealment, like a worm i' th' bud, / Feed on her damask cheek: she pined in thought, / And with a green and yellow melancholy / She sat like patience on a monument, / Smiling at grief." The answer begins with a blank: an empty page.

The main task is read mostly through the minus, through what the couple cannot yet do. The Sun's minus at this point is recognisable at once: what matters goes unsaid, feelings are kept in, people smile instead of speaking. Viola tells the truth, but about a "sister", in the third person, as if about the past. There is a confession, but no direct light.

Waite calls The Sun the light of consciousness — "the direct as the antithesis of the reflected light" — and writes of a child "in the sense of simplicity". Simplicity here is not naivety. It is the ability to say "I" where people say "a friend of mine", and "it hurts" where people say "it's fine".

In a couple this looks mundane. One partner puts up for years with something that hurts and jokes about it in front of friends. The other does not ask, because "it's all clear anyway". Resentment speaks in hints: a story about someone else's family, a sudden chill over dinner. The Sun in the minus can be loud as well. One partner shines for two and leaves the other no room: protects, decides, corrects. Or expects the partner to shine to their own script and snuffs them out when they fall short. Or disappears into work, where it is bright, while home stays in twilight. These are faces of one difficulty, not a description of a particular couple.

Olivia, once in love, puts the law of this tail into words: "A murd'rous guilt shows not itself more soon / Than love that would seem hid. Love's night is noon." Four words carry it: love's night is noon. In a play named after a night, this is the key. Hidden love shows anyway; the truth has long been in plain sight. The Sun does not need it uncovered. It needs it named.

sections.h2: The false sun: Malvolio in yellow stockings
paragraphs: The main task has a counterfeit double in the play. Olivia's steward Malvolio finds a letter planted by her gentlewoman Maria, who has forged her mistress's hand. Just before, Maria reports, "he has been yonder i' the sun practising behaviour to his own shadow this half hour." The letter says: "Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em," and the postscript: "in my presence still smile, dear my sweet, I prithee." Malvolio exults: "Daylight and champian discovers not more! This is open." And promises: "I will smile, I will do everything that thou wilt have me."

He comes to Olivia in yellow stockings, smiling to order. Maria reports: "He does smile his face into more lines than is in the new map with the augmentation of the Indies." Editors explain that a new map with both Indies drawn on it had recently been printed in England. A smile from someone else's script stretches a face into a map of the whole world. The World and The Sun, put together into a fake.

The play's first known spectator remembered exactly this. On 2 February 1602 the law student John Manningham saw Twelfth Night at a feast in the Middle Temple. In his diary he compared it to The Comedy of Errors and described one trick in detail: the steward was made to believe his lady was in love with him "by counterfeyting a letter as from his Lady", "prescribing his gesture in smiling, his apparaile". Of the whole comedy, the counterfeit sun is what went into the diary.

A 21-22-19 couple has its own Malvolio too, only it is not a person but a temptation. A smile instead of a conversation. Happy photos for everyone and "we're doing wonderfully" for the family. Expecting the partner to shine to a written script, and greatness that should simply drop onto the union. In Shakespeare this ends in a dark room where Malvolio is locked up as a madman, and with a line from the fool in a curate's gown: "there is no darkness but ignorance."

sections.h2: The Sun in Waite: two children hand in hand
paragraphs: Describing older decks, Waite mentions a Sun beneath which there is "a wall suggesting an enclosure—as it might be, a walled garden—wherein are two children, either naked or lightly clothed, facing a water, and gambolling, or running hand in hand." He himself chose another design, a child on a white horse, but he recorded the pair by the wall. The Sun of the old cards is not a lone hero in a spotlight but two in one light.

In Twelfth Night this pair appears in the last scene. Sebastian and Viola stand side by side for the first time, and the Duke cannot believe his eyes: "One face, one voice, one habit, and two persons! / A natural perspective, that is, and is not!" A "perspective" was the name for optical devices of lenses and mirrors that multiplied and distorted an image. Reflected light against direct light — Waite's key to The Sun, played on stage.

The numbers add one more pair of twins. In more than nine couples out of ten with this tail, The Sun of the main task is made of one partner's Justice (8) and the other's Strength (11): the main tasks of their personal tails. These are precisely the two cards that swap places in tarot history, like twins. Waite changed their numbers: "For reasons which satisfy myself, this card has been interchanged with that of Justice, which is usually numbered eight. As the variation carries nothing with it which will signify to the reader, there is no cause for explanation." The site uses the Marseille numbering: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength.

Our reading: this couple's light is gathered from one partner's sense of measure and the other's gentle strength. While the two are confused — the one who should weigh presses, the one who should hold keeps accounts — the result is a "natural perspective", double and untrue. When each stands in place, the result is The Sun. In another 6% of couples the same main task is made of The Hermit and The Wheel of Fortune (9 + 10).

sections.h2: The couple's centre: the Judgement missing from the tail
paragraphs: The tail 21-22-19 is made of the deck's last four cards minus one: 19, 21 and 22. One is missing — 20, Judgement. And that is the card that stands in the centre of the chart for 83.9% of such couples, in the sphere "The atmosphere inside the couple": what happens between the two when nobody is watching. The other 16.1% have 11, Strength, in the centre.

Benebell Wen opens her reading of the card with the words: "Key 20 is about spiritual awakening and epiphany." Epiphany is the very appearing whose eve gave the play its name. A couple with this tail lives through its own Twelfth Night, and in its centre the morning is already waiting.

In the play that morning comes like a resurrection. Sebastian comes to his sister as if out of the sea, and Viola tells him: "If spirits can assume both form and suit, / You come to fright us." He answers that, were she a woman, he would let his tears fall upon her cheek "And say, 'Thrice welcome, drowned Viola.'" They know each other by their father: a mole upon his brow, the day he died. Waite sees in Judgement a summons that "is heard and answered from within".

For the couple's atmosphere this means a great deal. In the plus: the feeling that the partner was not chosen but recognised; deep trust; the ability to forgive; a union with room for kin and family. In the minus, Judgement closes the two off from each other: neither dares to say what they feel, faults are sought in the other, warmth suddenly turns to cold. Even at the moment of recognition Viola holds back: "Do not embrace me till each circumstance / Of place, time, fortune, do cohere and jump / That I am Viola." Checking instead of embracing is a gesture this couple knows.
With Strength in the centre the atmosphere is different: the two charge and strengthen each other, tension turns into passion, and the difficulty lies in arguing over whose truth comes first.

sections.h2: A vow by the sun, and a dress nobody saw
paragraphs: The last scene. Still in a man's clothes, under the Duke's anger, Viola speaks of her love in front of everyone for the first time: she goes "After him I love / More than I love these eyes, more than my life". But these are still the words of the page Cesario. Once the secret is out, the Duke reminds her: "Boy, thou hast said to me a thousand times / Thou never shouldst love woman like to me." And Viola swears in her own name: "And all those sayings will I over-swear, / And all those swearings keep as true in soul / As doth that orbed continent the fire / That severs day from night." An orbed continent is a spherical container: the sun and each planet were thought to have one of their own. The heroine's first vow in her own person is a vow by the sun.

Set beside the fool's line, this vow reads like an answer. In Feste's words foolery walks about the orb like the sun and shines everywhere: scattered light that is everywhere and nowhere. In Viola's, the fire is held in its own sphere and divides day from night. The road from the middle of the tail to the main task fits into these two lines: from light spilled everywhere to light that tells things apart.

And at once, a delay. The Duke asks: "Give me thy hand, / And let me see thee in thy woman's weeds." The dress is with the captain, and the captain is in prison at Malvolio's suit. The wedding is put off until "golden time convents". The Duke's last words: "Cesario, come: / For so you shall be while you are a man; / But when in other habits you are seen, / Orsino's mistress, and his fancy's queen." The curtain falls before Viola appears as herself. Shakespeare left The Sun offstage.

What remains is Feste with his song about a rain that "raineth every day". Its last stanza begins "A great while ago the world begun": The World returns in the finale, and there is no sun on stage. The stanza about marriage runs: "But when I came, alas, to wive, / With hey, ho, the wind and the rain, / By swaggering could I never thrive." Wen writes of her Fool: "There is a trace of swagger and flamboyance in The Fool." The Fool's lightness suits the night of the feast. A marriage cannot live on it.

For the couple this is the play's main lesson. The main task is not solved on stage, in one brilliant evening. Viola's confession has already been made, and what follows is what is never acted: living as oneself every day, in ordinary daylight.

A tail that has been lived does not give up any of its cards. The World stays: the two still share a common language and big plans, but their world has doors — for friends, for family, for each partner's own pursuits. The Fool stays: trust, humour, lightness, the readiness to begin again. Only now the game has names, and both describe what they are to each other in the same words. And The Sun stops being a feat. It becomes everyday direct light: saying what hurt on the same day and without a joke; celebrating the partner's success out loud and not claiming it; letting oneself be seen tired, wrong, ridiculous.

In "The couple's values" 81.7% of such couples have The Lovers and 18.3% have The Devil. The Lovers is a choice made again and again, not once at the start. The Devil recalls the thought Lisovskaya draws from that card: nobody belongs to anybody. For a tail that begins with a world for two, this is an important correction.
What helps a couple with this tail:

ul: talking about what matters in the daytime, not at midnight and not between jokes;
calling the relationship what it is, and checking that both use the same name;
turning "travel the world" into a first step with a date;
noticing where a smile has replaced a conversation;
celebrating the partner's success out loud;
leaving room in the shared world for the people who love each of the two.

paragraphs: The strong version of tail 21-22-19 is Viola stepping out from the wings in her own dress, and the Duke looking at her in daylight. The play has no such scene. A couple can have one.

sections.h2: How the couple's tail 21-22-19 is calculated
paragraphs: The couple's matrix follows the school of Yuliana Lisovskaya: each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22 (if the sum is above 22, its digits are added). The example uses two dates: 14.08.1975 and 05.11.1975.

First date: day 14, month 8, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The tail's main task is 14 + 8 + 22 = 44 → 8, the centre 14 + 8 + 22 + 8 = 52 → 7, the entry 8 + 7 = 15, the middle 8 + 15 = 23 → 5. The personal tail is 15-5-8.
Second date: day 5, month 11, year 22. The main task is 5 + 11 + 22 = 38 → 11, the centre 5 + 11 + 22 + 11 = 49 → 13, the entry 11 + 13 = 24 → 6, the middle 11 + 6 = 17. The personal tail is 6-17-11.
The couple's tail adds up point by point:

This couple's centre is 7 + 13 = 20, Judgement, and "The couple's values" show 6, The Lovers. In this example The Sun also stands in "Image of the couple" (14 + 5) and in "What to create together" (8 + 11), but that belongs to these two dates, not to the whole tail.

The tail 21-22-19 occurs in about one couple in 113 (0.885%), 41st of the 97 couple tails. It comes from three combinations of personal tails: 15-5-8 and 6-17-11 in 92% of such couples, 18-9-9 and 3-13-10 in 6%, 15-8-11 and 6-14-8 in 1%.

The middle of the tail cannot be derived from the edges. The sum of the edges would give 21 + 19 = 40 → 4, while the couple's middle is 22: it is added up from the partners' middles. That is why there is no such personal tail: in a personal matrix the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 19 an entry of 21 would need a centre of 2, which no person has. Nor are there other couple tails made of the same three numbers: 21, 22 and 19 only ever come in this order.

ul: **21, The World — entry to the task.** This is where the couple begins: with the feeling that together they have a whole world — a common language, a shared outlook, plans without limits. The same wish can become a fence: a world for two that nobody else may enter.

**22, The Fool — middle of the task.** This is how the couple walks the road: with trust, lightness and play, with no ready-made form. The risk is going for years without naming what is happening between them.

**19, The Sun — main task.** To learn direct light: to speak about what matters in the first person, to show themselves to each other as they are, and not to replace a conversation with a smile and an "everything's fine".

intro: This tail has its own play. Around 1601 Shakespeare wrote the comedy Twelfth Night, or What You Will, and its plot runs exactly in the order of the three cards: a love the size of the world at the entry, a masquerade in the middle and an ending where everything hangs on one step into the light. The play never shows that step. And its fool says all three cards in a single sentence.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 21-22-19 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's matrix: entry to the task 21 (The World), middle 22 (The Fool), main task 19 (The Sun). The couple enters the task wanting a shared world, walks the road lightly and in play, and learns direct light: speaking about what matters in the first person and showing themselves to each other as they are.

faq.q: Is tail 21-22-19 a bad sign for a relationship?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not a verdict or a forecast. The main point is read through difficulty because it shows what the two have to learn. Lived through, the same three cards give a couple with a shared world, lightness and warm direct light.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 21-22-19 different from a personal tail?
faq.a: There is no personal tail 21-22-19: in a personal matrix such an entry with a main task of 19 would need a centre of 2. A couple's tail is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, so it has its own numbers and its own roles for the points.
No. From the numbers 21, 22 and 19 a couple's matrix only ever produces the order 21-22-19. This tail has no permutations among couples, so there is nothing to compare it with.

faq.q: How common is tail 21-22-19 among couples?
faq.a: About one couple in 113: 0.885% of all couples and 41st of the 97 couple tails. In 92% of such couples the partners come with the personal tails 15-5-8 and 6-17-11.

report: "Foolery, sir, does walk about the orb like the sun; it shines everywhere." This line from the fool in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night holds all three cards of the tail 21-22-19, in the same order: The World, The Fool, The Sun. It is said to a girl who spends the whole play in a mask. The plot of the comedy, written around 1601, follows the points of the couple's tail exactly: a love the size of the world at the entry, a masquerade in the middle and an ending where everything hangs on one step into the light.

Even the title is a clue. Twelfth Night is the last night of the Christmas season, the eve of Epiphany, a time of revelry when the usual order was turned upside down. The next morning came the feast of appearing. The play is named after the night before the light, and its second title, What You Will, simply means "whatever one wishes": the very thing a couple brings to the entry of its task.

report.h3: A love "more noble than the world" and a book opened in three days

report: The play opens in the voice of The World. Duke Orsino demands music — "Give me excess of it" — and says his love is "more noble than the world" and "all as hungry as the sea". Viola, disguised as the page Cesario, has served him for only three days, and he already tells her: "I have unclasp'd / To thee the book even of my secret soul." A whole world for two in three days. The start of a couple with this tail is recognisable here too: the feeling of having known each other all their lives, talk until dawn, one way of seeing things, plans "not like everyone else's".

But the entry to the task lies on the line of tasks, and the same wish becomes a fence. "I myself am best / When least in company," the Duke admits. Friends drift away; shared plans grow so big that they are frightening to start: the couple discusses a trip round the world, not next Tuesday. Each is sure the other already understands, so nothing has been agreed out loud. **Understanding is mistaken for an agreement.** The fool sums it up in one line that holds three words: everything, everywhere — and nothing.

Viola lives through the middle of the play as The Fool, and calls herself one: she tells Olivia "I am not what I am", and a moment later that she has become her fool. Page and master become best friends, but their closeness has no name. Who they are to each other nobody knows, themselves included.

For a couple with The Fool in the middle this means trust, humour, freedom, the ability to start from zero. And the same lightness in the minus: years together, and still "we just live together". A serious talk turns into a joke, a conflict is solved by a move or a new project, and at the step that requires naming the relationship in front of witnesses, the two step back. The fool in the play jokes that "fools are as like husbands as pilchards are to herrings". **The middle of this tail stands exactly between play and marriage.**

The quietest scene is the most exact one for the main task. Viola tells the Duke about her "father's daughter" who loved and kept silent: "A blank, my lord. She never told her love… She sat like patience on a monument, / Smiling at grief." The truth is told, but about a "sister", in the third person. There is a confession, but no direct light.

This is The Sun's minus at the main point: what matters goes unsaid, feelings are kept in, people smile instead of speaking. Waite calls The Sun "the direct as the antithesis of the reflected light" and writes of a child "in the sense of simplicity". **Simplicity means saying "I" where people say "a friend of mine", and "it hurts" where people say "it's fine".** The Sun in the minus can be loud as well: one partner shines for two and leaves the other no room, expects the other to shine to a script, or disappears into work, where it is bright, while home stays in twilight.

The same play has a counterfeit sun. The steward Malvolio, following a planted letter, smiles at his mistress as instructed, and before that "he has been yonder i' the sun practising behaviour to his own shadow this half hour." The play's first known spectator, John Manningham, wrote exactly this trick into his diary in 1602: how the steward was told how to smile. A smile instead of a conversation, happy photos for everyone, "we're doing wonderfully" for the family: a couple with this tail has its own Malvolio, not a person but a temptation.

Olivia states the law that cancels all of this: hidden love shows as surely as guilt, and "Love's night is noon." Four words. What is hidden is already in plain sight. The Sun needs not an exposure but a word.

In the finale Viola swears in her own name for the first time, and she swears by the sun: she will keep her vows "As doth that orbed continent the fire / That severs day from night." The fool's foolery shone everywhere, scattered. Viola's fire is held in its own sphere and divides day from night. The road from the middle of the tail to the main task fits into these two lines.

And at once, a delay. The Duke asks to see her in her woman's weeds, but the dress is with the captain, and the captain is in prison. The wedding is put off until "golden time convents", and the Duke leads her away still calling her Cesario. **The curtain falls before Viola appears as herself: Shakespeare left The Sun offstage.** The main task is not solved in one brilliant evening. It begins where the performance ends: living as oneself every day, in ordinary light.

A tail that has been lived does not give up any of its cards. The shared world stays, but it gains doors for friends, for family, for each partner's own pursuits. The game stays, but it gains names, and both describe what they are to each other in the same words. And The Sun becomes an everyday thing: saying what hurt on the same day and without a joke; celebrating the partner's success out loud; turning "travel the world" into a first step with a date; noticing where a smile has replaced a conversation.

unit.meaning: Your task is to step into direct light: speak about what matters in the first person and not let a smile stand in for talk.
